utterances.text: We all called him Sprzo. We all knew him as Sprzo. I think his real name was Maric. He shot not at the pensioners' hall, but he did shoot at the building and in the air. And members of the police went out and, like, walked him along. You can imagine what kind of scene that was. Mandic and I stayed together for quite a while after that meeting in the pensioners' hall. We had coffee and a few drinks, and we tried to find solutions, and both of us saw that things were not funny anymore. It was the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the chief of the public security station was Savo Tepic at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He came to the position of chief of SJB after the elections in 1990 and in keeping with the election agreement between national parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That would mean that Savo Tepic took over as chief of the public security station of Kotor Varos in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as the parties agreed and the new authorities were put in place, Savo Tepic took over as chief of the police station immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means that his election as chief of SJB was supported both by HDZ and the SDA parties. It was an agreement?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an agreement. Everybody supported his election. Nobody had objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The actual decision to appoint him as chief of the public security station of Kotor Varos was issued by the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, headed by Minister Alija Delimustafic, who belonged to the SDA party, the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at that time were there any objections from Sarajevo, from the government, from the ministry, to the election of Savo Tepic as chief of the security station in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember any objections. There was only one suggestion, namely, that it would be desirable to have a person graduated in humanities rather than engineering. Savo was an engineer. And they wanted three nominees for that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Savo Tepic, when he was appointed in 1990 by the ministry, which was headed by minister Alija Delimustafic, who was a member of the SDA party, he was an engineer who basically had no experience with policing whatsoever at the time, at least directly, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When conflict erupted, that is, in May-June 1992, Savo Tepic remained chief and which had -- in the position where he had been since 1990; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There were no changes to that effect, were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no changes as to the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for providing these answers, and I apologise to you that you had to wait so long. It wasn't up to us and nor was it the will of the Chamber. It was merely a result of circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. On behalf of the Defence of Stojan Zupljanin, I'm going to ask you a few questions. I apologise for saying "Slobodan" instead of "Stojan." We tend to get -- we tend to confuse those two names. So I'm going to ask you a few questions about your previous testimony and about your testimony that you gave today. Mr. Djekanovic, in replying to the questions of my learned friend, Mr. Zecevic, about the events preceding the outbreak of conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you spoke about the session held on the 14th of October, 1991, you said so to the Prosecutor when the Serbian Members of Parliament walked out of the parliament hall because they were down voted by Muslim and Croat Members of Parliament. Do you remember those events?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is the position of the Defence that that very event, that down voting, was the crucial moment because the constitutional rights of the Serbian people had been infringed upon, and that's what incited the avalanche in Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood what went on at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with regard to the position of the Serbian people the members of the Muslim-Croat coalition had a similar plan as to that which had been going on in Croatia previously. First they changed the constitution and deleted the Serbs from the constitution as a constitutive people in Croatia, and thereby deprived them of their basic rights; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that started the avalanche of conflict in Croatia, and so that similar scenario was to be expected in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was obviously being prepared; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for Bosnia-Herzegovina too. There had been several attempts to preserve -- at least Bosnia or keep it within Yugoslavia. You probably remember Muhamed Filipovic who tried to strike agreements in Belgrade but there were other initiatives too, but they all came to nothing, and things developed in the direction that you outlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the constituting of the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all these organs was a direct outcome of that parliamentary session and the behaviour of the Muslim-Croat coalition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, it was a direct outcome and -- because the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been infringed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the constituting of your own Serbian Assembly and the attempts to protect the rights of Serbs and organise themselves better within Bosnia-Herzegovina to the extent it was possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to add that in my sincere opinion we had always been forced to do things. We were always lagging behind things. We never had the initiative to start something. We always reacted to something that had already happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in reality with regard to the coalition agreement after the multi-party elections, you as a member of your party did not expect the subsequent development and you weren't prepared?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the SDS was not prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what I have briefly outlined is your conviction and your view of the events in which you took part and which you witnessed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, speaking about the establishment of Crisis Staffs, I may have overlooked something but I believe that you answered to the Prosecutor that Crisis Staffs had been established in the Kotor Varos municipality much before these events, namely, the arrival of refugees from Croatia; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some form of Crisis Staff we had much earlier, both us and the others, earlier than the dates that are mentioned as the dates of establishment because we had -- we had taken action before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you met for the first time to try to help the refugees who were coming from Croatia in the course of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first concrete activity was helping to accommodate these people and the municipal organisation of the Red Cross, gathering aid for those people such as food, clothing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, can you explain the Chamber the notion of Crisis Staff? It goes to mean that it's a body that established in a crisis situation, others -- in an extraordinary circumstances, when things are beyond normal. So that is the essence of both the name and of the function of the Crisis Staff, irregular circumstances; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. So there must be extraordinary circumstances and events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the establishment of the Crisis Staff you understood to be an activity to ensure normal functioning of the municipality and its bodies until regular -- regular bodies are established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in the work of the Crisis Staff and the subsequent period, not only members of the SDS took part in that but also persons who were not SDS members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SDS membership was not essential. We wanted people who worked in certain areas, who did certain jobs, but I would like to add that once the conflict started in Croatia we then had legal authorities in Kotor Varos. But a dozen people or so had already been killed in Croatia as fighters fighting in the ranks of the JNA who -- which was established under the laws and the constitution of the SFRY. So we had people from Kotor Varos who had been killed, and we also took -- we also took care of such activities in order to assist the families of those killed to bury their dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the municipal bodies of the -- of Kotor Varos were not able to get involved, but you tried to assist the families in burying their dead?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we did because the -- in -- the municipality prefect did not want us to do anything so that the executive committee of the municipality did not pass any decision to that effect. So we as a Crisis Staff assisted the families to bury their killed family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I'll try to make an effort, but you make an effort too because we speak the same language for behalf of -- or rather for the sake of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I will make an effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, in replying to the Prosecutor's question you confirmed that on the 12th of May, 1992, you attended the Assembly of the Republika Srpska in Banja Luka. Do you remember speaking about that session? When the VRS was founded and a number of important decisions for the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina was passed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I attended that session, but what was decided there was brought -- was brought to my mind again only after seeing the relevant minutes. But yes, I was there and I know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up on e-court Exhibit P74. Your Honours, we have a problem with e-court here. Mr. Pantelic took part in resolving the problem that we had with the OTP, but there is a part which is not in e-court and it is important for this questioning today. So Mr. Pantelic, who was involved in correcting the error in e-court will now take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... with our learned friends from OTP, and Mr. Smith told us that it will be corrected -- actually, what we see here on the screen are the original minutes of the whole session of the Assembly, but prior to this page we have four pages of actually minutes in shortened form with agenda. So we have it in English language, these four pages, but apparently they are missing in B/C/S language. So for the purpose of the next numbers I think -- questions, maybe our friend from OTP can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're just checking. It's quite right, it was brought to our attention. We're just checking to see whether it was corrected. It may not have been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case what I could suggest is that we could have on e-court pages -- previous pages of the document in English, the ERN number is 0091-3501 up to 04. So we could have English version and then with the help of interpreters maybe my friend can just brought attention of this witness to certain portions and then we could have it in transcript. And then on a later stage our friends I'm sure will download this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- few pages in B/C/S. I think that would be a solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what happened was that what we did originally is we took out the English pages so that the B/C/S and English corresponded. We haven't yet put back the English and the B/C/S. So at the moment, I'm sorry, I'm afraid we can't assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It can be resolved like that. My friend will go through these particular points, and then the witness will comment, and then in later stage they can put. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, could now please ERN number 0091-3501 be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, this is what this is about, there is a minor mismatch between the English translation and the original because the agenda is missing. I want to show you a part of the agenda and the decision that was taken with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. We can pull up the B/C/S but we can't pull up the English at that moment, I'm afraid. We've got the first few pages in B/C/S, so it's going to have to be the other way around -- oh, it's in Sanction at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under item 3, confirmation of the decisions and other regulations passed by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BiH. Do you remember that some of these were actually confirmed at this parliamentary session? I will later continue.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the practice for the Assembly to confirm the decisions that the Presidency had passed at a moment when the Assembly -- when it wasn't possible to call an Assembly. But I can hardly remember any one particular decision, but yes that was the practice to proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the next page of this document, please. The next page. The B/C/S version differs from the English copy that I have in my hand, so the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we need the third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, do look what it says under item 7, the decision on the proclamation of imminent threat of war. That is one of decisions that was confirmed by the Assembly, that there is an imminent threat of war in the territory of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I see, item 7 reads that the Assembly adopted the bill about the amendments of the law on people's defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat. The interpreter didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that there was discussion about taking some measures about this decision?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was much decision about this item. I know that there was much discussion about why not to immediately proclaim the state of war rather than an imminent threat of war, but I don't remember the details anyway. This is what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the interpretation I must repeat once more. So here at this session the decision on the proclamation of the imminent threat of war in the territory of Republika Srpska was passed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, as far as the situation is concerned I will now take you back to the start of wartime activities in the municipality of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this document should be an exhibit, I believe that we can resolve the issue in direct communication with the OTP. So for these documents to become part of Exhibit P47, so that for the time being I will not tender this part of the document if that is acceptable. I see that the OTP are nodding in agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, you were saying in replying to the questions asked by both the OTP and Mr. Zecevic, you were speaking about the conflicts in the municipality of Kotor Varos in 1992. Let me take you back to the start. It is obvious that all the events that happened in June were preceded by tension and sporadic conflicts among members of all three ethnicities in Kotor Varos, the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And all three sides had set up guards, barricades, everybody was mindful to protect their village or hamlet or street because there was an atmosphere of fear, as there had already been conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this also calls for an amendment. Both I and Anto Mandic and Fikret, from SDA, Abdic did visit the guards because we knew where -- who had guards where. SDA had some guards in the streets that they controlled, and that man stayed at Kotor Varos throughout the war. I will not say that he didn't have any problems, but he didn't have problems that could have occurred, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do slow down a little because the interpreters cannot keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I got carried away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you, but I have to remind you to go a bit slower. Could you please repeat this part.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So everybody had their guards. In the town itself the guards were separated. There were attempts to have joint guards, but that didn't succeed, but we knew who had guards in which streets. And I said that on one occasion or several, but I do remember one clearly we went to see those guards together, and we went to the Muslim guards in lower Kotor Varos. So that was the situation at the time. Everybody had their own guards, they were -- everybody was scared, but unfortunately everybody was also preparing for the worst, namely, for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And before the events of mid-June 1992, there were movements of the population so that some Serb inhabitants of the outskirts of the municipality that were encircled by Croatian villages started moving into Kotor Varos; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the 11th of June here as the date when the Serbian forces decided to take full control, let's say in the municipality of Kotor Varos. Can you tell us something about the incidents that preceded these events and what was the immediate cause for the decision to take control in the municipality of Kotor Varos? Do you recall the incidents that preceded that act? I'm going to focus you on two of them, the one in Sipovici and the one in Vasiljevici, can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were other things happening in the course of May, other than those two incidents. There was an attempt by all three of the national parties to organise a public forum where we were supposed to assemble the public intelligence and the political elite of Kotor Varos and to make an effort to avoid the war conflict. The idea was to hold this meeting in the Kotor Varos cinema, but the SDA and the HDZ went behind our backs and made a completely different arrangement. So instead of setting it up in the cinema in Kotor Varos they organised it in the sports stadium of Kotor Varos and invited their own sympathisers. So there was a lot of provocations that took place, and then behind that location armed members of the HVO were walking around and stories were already circulating in town almost every evening how these two parties would take over power in Kotor Varos at the time this evening or that evening. In any case, there was a lot of fear among all sides. And then the prevailing opinion on our side was that it was about time to do something ourselves instead of getting caught out. Before that things happened, not only the ones that you referred to, there were barricades being set up in several places, the ones followed by ultimatums. And I recall very well that I went with members of the police, with Anto Mandic, to this village of Vecici to speak with people and how it was difficult to get out there of that village. People were up in the trees and there were barricades so it was difficult to get out. And then this killing of this family happened. I don't remember the exact date, and I think the court case is being brought to its completion for the murder of a family in Glamoc by the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were killings also in other hamlets and villages around Vecici. There were small settlements or hamlets settled by Serbs, and so there were some shootings and provocations happening in those areas too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one correction, we're talking about the killing of the Glamocak family, not a family from Glamoc. So we're talking about the killing of the Glamocak family in the village of Sipovi [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they were of Serb ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a person called Neskobic [phoen] was sentenced to the Bosnia and Herzegovina court to a sentence of nine years. I read this in the newspaper. Does that refer to this incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does refer to this incident. I don't know if this was a final decision, but I know that a judgement was passed and the sentence too. I don't know if the person is actually -- has began to serve his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then this killing in the village of Vasiljevici, this happened sometime before the take-over of power?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasiljevici is a hamlet above the village of Vecici and this is where the killing happened in that period of time. The communication with the municipality -- actually, the road passed through the village of Vecici that led to our municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Mr. Krgovic continues, can I just raise one matter. I've discussed this with my learned friends in the break. Mr. Zecevic concluded his cross-examination without putting to the witness at all that when he said - and I'm looking at the transcript on the 8th of October, Thursday, at page 1101 and 1102 - that the Crisis Staff did not have the authority to order the police, we could not issue orders to the police. We did not have the right to do that. That was not challenged, and I asked if that evidence was accepted because if it's not challenged we're entitled to assume it's accepted, and Mr. Zecevic says it is not accepted. In which case I said that then that must be put to the witness that he's not right when he says that. And I understand Mr. Zecevic has a problem with that which perhaps he can explain. But, Your Honours, I think it's important that this is dealt with now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two aspects of this. Aspect number one is I believe during the cross-examination the witness said -- I cannot find it right now in the transcript, but if you give me some time I will. I was asking him, "Did you have the overall power as a Crisis Staff on the municipality?" He says, "Yes, except for the military matters." That is -- as far as I am concerned that is actually counter to what he said in the direct examination, where he was saying that he didn't control either the police or the military. Today he said only military. As far as I'm concerned, this is a challenge of what he says -- what he said to my learned friend in the -- during the direct -- cross-examination. Therefore, I didn't want to pursue the matter anymore. We had the documents which confirmed that they were giving, in fact, orders to the police. That's one aspect. The other aspect, Your Honours, again we're coming back to the issue of he -- him being a suspect. If I ask him, "Did you control -- did you order the police?" And he says, "Yes," he's incriminating himself. I mean, this has to be again in a sense addressed. We need to know how to proceed in these situations. That is my comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I mean -- I can certainly deal if Mr. Zecevic and Your Honours take the view that that's sufficient, we controlled everybody except the military say the police, then I can deal with that in re-examination and go back to what on the face of it is now contradictory answers. But I don't think that in itself is sufficient to put to a witness that a clear and one of the few unambiguous statements he made is not accepted. So that's the first thing. As to the second point, Your Honours, with the greatest of respect I don't think Your Honours should be considering what any position may be in any other court. For the moment I'm just leaving it. I'm hoping to get information to put before Your Honours to show that any suggestion that this can be used, that answers which might incriminate him and which he's told to answer in this court can be used against him in subsequent proceedings in another court is incorrect. I've made certain inquiries to confirm my own knowledge, but at the moment I can't put something before Your Honours. But it's absolutely clear in any event in the law that Mr. Zecevic quoted to you that evidence can be excluded if it is more prejudicial than probative and clearly if an answer was, as it were, forced out, he was forced to answer a question which might incriminate him that would come within that aspect of the law. But in any event we would argue that what may happen in another court is not for Your Honours to concern yourself with at the moment. But, Your Honours, I think the better point is: Do Your Honours feel that that is sufficient that today he only mentioned the military and not the police in the light of what he said earlier and I believe said twice in chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner and Mr. Zecevic, obviously the control which the Crisis Staff had over the police is an essential issue. This is very obvious from the case, so we thought that it might actually be helpful to the Chamber if that point could be taken up just to clarify the answer that he gave to you this morning because we all -- it turns out that all three Judges took exactly that note, that he said that he had control over everything except the military. So I think if we can ask Mrs. Korner to bring it up and to clarify with the witness while he's here and -- but to do so in a manner that doesn't lure him into a trap that may later on be held against him if criminal proceedings are raised in other courts. I -- I'm not going to engage in a discussion about this fact, but I think that there is a potential for using testimonies before this Tribunal as evidence in other courts. So I think Mr. Zecevic during his cross-examination steered very skillfully around the issues that might become difficult for the witness later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, -- yes, I'm sorry, but he didn't -- he doesn't -- I don't think he wants the answer, as I wouldn't if I were defending. But as Your Honours say, it's such an important matter that if the Defence case is he is not telling the truth or is mistaken about that, it has to be properly put. But -- and proceedings in other courts, I'm afraid, should not be troubling this Trial Chamber because although of course were he could be prosecuted for his part in these events, what he says here will go. The judges there do have a discretion under their laws to exclude evidence. And I'm aware that that has been done, and I can put it no higher than that at the moment. But my point is simply, and it's one that will affect future witnesses, if something is not accepted by a defendant of such importance to an issue in the case then it must be put in clear terms. But I am perfectly willing to deal with this in re-examination. My only query is what happens if in re-examination he says now I couldn't give orders and that's not the case. But anyhow, Your Honours, there's one other matter which the Registrar raised with me, apparently he's due to fly back this afternoon. I do have to deal with that in re-examination and two other matters which he dealt with that came out as a result of cross-examination. I don't know how much longer Mr. Krgovic has got, but it seems to me he may not be able to fly back if we're stopping at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There is -- there are 60 minutes left, Mr. Krgovic. How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour, to conclude my cross-examination before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is to say you're going to use the next hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. Depends on the answer, but I got -- the very narrow issues of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I mean, in that case he won't be able to leave? We're sorry we have to contact --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he won't unless we use -- the only suggestion I had, Your Honours, is if we've got Court III and if we're going to have interpreters perhaps we could finish him off at 2.15 this afternoon if it's just ten minutes' worth of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Registrar informs us that it will take too long time to set up Courtroom III for this purpose. So the only way in which we can conclude his testimony is by, once again, turning to the interpreters. And I'm really not very happy about having to do that because I think the interpreters are carrying such a huge load for us and I would feel bad about having to ask them once again to sit here for another half hour or whatever it takes to finish it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Obviously, he'll have to stay and just be here for tomorrow morning then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm afraid so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think, Your Honour -- obviously this is important, as Your Honours realise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So we will adjourn at 1.45, as scheduled, and hope that we can then finish Witness 181 off tomorrow morning. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the witness is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, let us continue where we left off before the break. Just one clarification. When I asked you about the villages and the incident in the village of Vasiljevici specifically, the village of Vasiljevici is a Serb village, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the shepherd who was killed in the village of Vasiljevici was a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, you spent a lot of time talking about the situation in Kotor Varos in 1992, and I'm going to just say in a few words how I understood your words. It was war in the territory of municipality of Kotor Varos. There were many people killed, wounded, refugees on all three sides. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Lack of consumer articles, the presence of different military formations in the municipality area, constant tension. In brief it was an actual state of war, an actual war situation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the functioning of the municipal organs and all other organs was guided by those conditions, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation corresponded to the conditions that prevailed. There was no agreement. It was impossible to come to any kind of decision. The organs of power were not functioning. I said that the -- each chief of police was informing his own people in Sarajevo, Banja Luka; the Croats were informing their people, I'm talking about the police chiefs. So it was a difficult situation and the war had engulfed practically the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the 11th of June, a fierce conflict broke out in the Kotor Varos area as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of June you could really say that there were no conflicts really. There were no killings, no re-settlement of the population. Everybody was rallying around their own groups. There were no killings on the 11th itself, and that can even apply to the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But then after the combat began in the areas around Kotor Varos and Kotor Varos itself, general conflict broke out in the whole of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And there were many casualties as a result of that conflict; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm just going to give you a piece of information speaking about the strength of the Croat-Muslim coalition. It's a fact saying that 400 people were killed and 650 people were wounded during the combat in Kotor Varos until the situation calmed down. I'm speaking about Serbian casualties.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's accurate data about the casualties. I cannot really tell you how many Serbs were killed in the territory of Croatia before the conflicts here broke out, but overall there were about 400 killed victims in the area of Kotor Varos and there was a large number of the wounded, many of whom were actually civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this number who were actually killed in Croatia, I mean it's about ten-odd people that we're talking about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the situation calmed down somewhat in June, the Muslim-Croat formations changed their tactics and began to set up ambushes and carry out attacks along the roads, moving on to a kind of guerilla-type conflict in the entire municipality of Kotor Varos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it was normal that the units of the Territorial Defence and the army had to carry out military actions in order to neutralise these units that were in the areas around Kotor Varos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first seven, eight, or ten days the line actually was in the town itself. The Vrbanja river was a front line, and in the town itself we had people who were killed by sniper fire from snipers firing around -- positions around the town of Kotor Varos from neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As a result of those actions and the conflict between the Croat-Muslim and Serb forces, the civilian population withdrew from those villages and entered the town. This is what I understood from your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A smaller number of people came to town, where the bulk actually through their representatives in the negotiations, sought to move out and leave the area of the Kotor Varos municipality, and this is -- this situation in which these convoys were formed which some people are interpreting in this way and some people are interpreting in another way. But we believed that they were the best way to protect a substantial part of the population, and these convoys were the means by which people left to other parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was essential to remove those people from combat zones because the fighting there was continual and there were ambushes and attacks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was essential and the people themselves wanted to leave those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There were ambushes in that period in which Colonel Stevilovic was killed and Markovic who was a police official. This was in an -- in a road ambush, and they were killed and massacred?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an ambush and the two of them were killed, along with one other civilian -- actually, they had given a ride to two civilians in their car. The three of them were not only killed but they were butchered. Their skulls were smashed. The car was riddled with bullets and one of the civilians was captured and taken with the attackers, and he spent about a month or so on enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this was followed by a military action attacking Croat-Muslim positions and the fighting continued, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In any case there was a military response against the Vecici settlement. I don't remember whether it was on that occasion because there was several attacks that ensued on that road where civilians were killed and wounded. In one of those attacks on the village of Vecici a group was arrested. I don't know how many of them, but I did see them with my own eyes when they were brought in. So a group of soldiers was arrested. Some were killed, some were arrested, and after a long negotiation about the wounded soldiers they were brought in a tractor-trailer which was loaded with a whole pile of bodies that were scorched that had been in a fire that were massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another question that has to do with this area. In Croat-Muslim villages there were no conflicts. You told the Prosecutor about those villages, and you showed those villages on a map for the Prosecutor. There was no movement of population or armed conflicts in those villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't say that nobody left those villages. Individually people did leave, but the bulk of villagers stayed in Siprage and Barici and other villages. The bulk of those inhabitants stayed. A significant portion of the Muslim population also remained in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So I understand that what you understood of the situation is that Muslim civilians were evacuated only from those villages that were in conflict and those villages where there was no conflict no population really left the villages?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in any case nowhere were the civilians removed by force. In any place where stability could be maintained and where people wanted to stay, they stayed. I have firm evidence of that, I have witnesses, I have written material and statement, but that is not the topic of what we're talking about now. In any case, there was security for those people in Marici [as interpreted], in Siprage, people were in those villages. I don't know that any excess or any incident occurred. I haven't heard of anything out of the ordinary taking place in such villages. Mostly they were safe where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As a result of the killing of those Serb civilians, the tensions grew in town itself. There was pressure from victims' families on you. There were cases of retaliation and revenge against some members of the Croat-Muslim forces. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that was the situation. It was unbearable and looking at it from now I think we did quite well to go through all of that. I did refer to those families a couple of days ago during my testimony. There were days when we would bury 12 or 16 people. There was no day that would pass without funerals. And on top of all the things that we had to do in that period most of our work actually had to do with organising funerals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know what happened --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that was the result and a response, but I don't justify such a response. But it did happen. It's true that the evening before in this village of Kotor across the Vrbanja river some people were killed. While they were asleep a bomb was thrown into the bedroom as they were sleeping and then there was this reaction, military reaction in the morning. And then as a consequence of this military action is what happened among a sector of those people, but I don't justify those actions in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My question was not recorded. I asked about this incident in the health centre. Your reply was the reply to this question?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Local people were killed in their sleep, people from Kotor?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a number of people were brought from Kotor where this incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, you described in your prior testimony the rising of tensions between various police forces, military forces, lack of coordination in their work, mutual apportioning of blame. Was that what was happening in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially in the last days of June -- sorry, the whole of June and the first ten days of July. There was a great shortage of coordination and very poor linkage between forces in military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That made you quite angry. What happened when one such action led to the death of a number of people because it was poorly coordinated?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one example. It was another military action in that part of town near Kotor. We had information that up to noon we were to expect our first military success. Then a number of commanders went each their own way, made themselves scarce. Things ran out of control and things took a completely different turn. Some people got wounded, an ambulance went to fetch them, the staff of the ambulance vehicle including the driver was killed, some people were captured. Complete chaos ensued in town but also in the units on the territory of Kotor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was why you addressed Stojan Zupljanin at that picnic, that lunch you had, you mentioned it before?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed not only Stojan Zupljanin, but also Mr. Peu lic and the other Zupljanin who was commander of some unit. So it was a broader discussion, not just one on one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just let me clarify this, although I understand it from your interview and your testimony. When you discussed all these matters, that was the only conversation of that kind you had with Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps at some other points in 1992 towards the end we met more frequently when the Assembly started to work. But in June and July, that was the only occasion I spoke to him apart from the contacts we had or were supposed to have through the War Presidency, and the chief of the public security station Savo Tepic also took part in this. I don't remember that we had any more discussions on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this was practically the main subject because you were quite concerned and very upset over what happened. You expressed your dissatisfaction over the lack of coordination and the general military situation in your area?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, and we made no secret of our views, and we also imparted to them the positions taken by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the OTP, the Prosecution asked you about the date of this meeting, whether this meeting happened before the incident at the health centre or after, and you said you couldn't remember. You still can't remember, can you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give you a time-line of these events. I did not keep any documents. I did not keep record. I'm not that kind of person. I just cannot give you the chronological order of these events, whether it was before or after the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In that broader discussion, that informal talk over lunch, you addressed all those present, not specifically Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a group of us sort of went to one side. I don't think I actually stayed for lunch. We just went to one side and discussed this, the people I've already enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not discuss specific incidents. You spoke of problems and incidents. You did not go like, this happened in this and that place in such and such a time. It was in general terms?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed in general terms the problems we were facing and the need to coordinate that, to put these things under control so that nothing like that happens again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you probably said that this communication with Zupljanin should go through Savo Tepic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that. To me it was a normal line of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned Savo Tepic. You knew him. What kind of person is he? Is he a straightforward person who would readily share information with you and with others? What sort of contact did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Tepic tends to keep things to himself. Later on he was reluctant to get involved and share information that he actually could have shared. When we would sit down and talk he was always rather grim, in a bad mood. And we even had a problem over these disagreements and this lack of readiness to cooperate, and even though we didn't want to interfere with the work of the police it led to incidents. Savo Tepic didn't like interference, and we did not interfere. So even if we did not always give him as much support as we -- as he should have liked, we certainly didn't interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And even when he attended official meetings or failed to attend them, you always had the impression, didn't you, that he was making pretexts in order not to go?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can understand that. I know that on the one hand you are supposed to go to Banja Luka to attend these meetings, and you never get any feedback from him. If a person really wants to they can always find a means to get there. At least in June and July he was a very frightened man. He barely ever left the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This -- what you just said is about Savo Tepic because it's not clear from the record?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Savo Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he had a nickname "Very Urgent" because he would always say he had something urgent to attend to but never said any more about it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, our colleagues on the Crisis Staff called him "Very Urgent." There was a label on documents in MUP, and he would often say, "I'm urgently, very urgently, required elsewhere," and he would use it as a pretext to leave the session of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about this incident outside the health centre, you didn't have any detailed information about what was going on. You just heard from the director that some people were murdered?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I just got a report at Crisis Staff, and of course there was more talk later that reached me. But the first report I got from the director of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You did not know who the perpetrators were or any other facts?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never found out the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And various stories circulated that those were irregular units, all local units, but you never found out for certain who killed those people?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I know that people talked, some of our own local people talked, that these murders were committed by members of special units. But I cannot imagine that Rajko Skoric was mentioned as a possible perpetrator in some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Correction -- sorry, the witness didn't say that it was special units, but local units.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that -- out about that later. At first we just got a preliminary report at the Crisis Staff that some people were killed. But then various stories started circulating around town, and there were suspicions against various people and some names began to be mentioned, including Rajko Skoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you learned later that some of the locals took part in this killing?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I learned that some of the locals were present on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you heard that much later because there was no one like Savo Tepic to report to you and say what happened was this and that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the Crisis Staff we really had no details. We did not know either the number of people who were killed or the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it's possible that if local people were involved, that information would be kept back from you and those real perpetrators would try to blame someone else?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were of course attempts to shift blame, but those were times when nobody really assumed any responsibility, and no one had the time to investigate thoroughly. It was never a priority, not even for us. We never made a decision to investigate the whole matter through and through. But we did try to prevent anything like that from happening again. And actually, I can't recall any more incidents on that scale. There was perhaps one more minor incident later. There was a couple of incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you in the Crisis Staff did your best to prevent further incidents of the sort?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We absolutely tried, and I believe there is evidence of that, and I think you can freely say that as of mid-July no such things happened again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you urged members of the police, the army, and other forces to work on it, to prevent such things?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the last part of your answer was: And we did achieve good results?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think our efforts really resulted in something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, the OTP asked you a series of questions about commanding that special unit. You said then that, both in your interview and here, that you weren't sure who of them was the commander. If I were to put to you that the commander of that unit was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have a reference to the page in the interview, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It takes some time, Your Honour, because my learned colleague mentioned that in examination-in-chief but -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to delay matters, but perhaps Mr. Krgovic can point it out to me when he's finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't heard, can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you are going to ask about "that special unit." What special unit do you mean? I don't see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The unit that was in Kotor Varos, that's what I meant, Your Honours, and its commanding personnel. The unit that was in Kotor Varos in the summer of 1991, a special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, do you know by any chance that that unit was commanded by Captain Lukic, member of the 1st Krajina Corps, and that that unit had a mixed composition. It consisted of both military units and police units, and they also had military IDs. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be -- I must sincerely admit that I didn't know all those details. I don't know them now even, so I cannot really corroborate what you said with any certainty. I said on the last day when I was questioned here that I don't know whether that unit even was completely manned or whether it was just part of a larger unit. I heard of Mr. Lukic, but whether or not he was the commander of that special unit I must admit I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We're talking about a police unit. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our position differs somewhat from that of the OTP. We consider that unit not to have been a purely police unit -- I'm sorry, I apologise. It really wasn't my intention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is exactly the reason why I asked, because I want to make sure that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have stated my case now that is the position of the Defence, but I do apologise for that. I really try not to make speeches here and put forward my own positions when trying to obtain evidence, but it does happen. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djekanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let us elicit from the witness again what is his views on the identity of this special unit. Was it a special police unit or a special military unit or a special unit of volunteers or TO or where are we? What kind of special unit was it? Can you help us understand this, Mr. Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this question. I know for sure that among those people who were in Kotor Varos there were some who had never been with the police. I even mentioned the name of Slobodan Dubocanin, and I know that he has never been a police officer. And it seemed to me -- seems strange to me too for such a person to command a police unit, and there are others who had never been with the police. So I cannot really -- I don't really know what to make of all that, but some people from our municipality joined that unit later. I know that so -- I know instances of that to have happened, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I -- Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic have just suggested to me that with regard to the OTP's remark of putting forward our own position, that I should try to elicit through the witness about the relations between the police and the Crisis Staff and that sort of thing. So if you allow, I would like to clarify that with the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do, but I see that we are actually a bit ahead of our time, and if we could conclude the testimony of this witness today I'm sure it would be very helpful. Mr. Krgovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't conclude my re-examination today, particularly in the view of the very last answers and the fact that I've got to now check the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Krgovic, please carry on with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I apologise but I will ask for some more of your time. Many documents have been shown to you and tendered into evidence, and they pertain to the relations between the Crisis Staff and the police in the municipality of Kotor Varos, and in our conclusions as to the relations between all Crisis Staffs and the security forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I will focus on this aspect of the relations between the police and the Crisis Staff, and I will show you some documents and put forward our position with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness the 65 ter document number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the Registrar could help me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 00690.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document has already been admitted as Exhibit 1D24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, the document is about to appear on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, take a careful look at the document. You have seen these documents briefly when they were introduced, but now I'll ask you to read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order to impose a curfew in Kotor Varos municipality. This is a decision of the Crisis Staff, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here you're actually issuing an order as this document reads. "The Crisis Staff hereby issues an order to the Army of the Serbian Republic of BiH ..." That's what it says?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, beyond a doubt this is what it says, and the Crisis Staff consisted of all of us so it was our joint decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a joint decision taken by you and the police?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a decision by the Crisis Staff because it was within the remit of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But it was also -- it also includes some powers, that is, some remit of the police, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it comes to implementation. But it refers not only to the police but also to military structures, that is, those controlling the security situation in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I understood this document, you - the Crisis Staff - are ordering to the police and the military to implement some decisions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this decision was necessary for everybody, the military, the police, and the questioning so far I have said that there was a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness Exhibit P86, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt but an urgent matter has come up, and as this witness is going to have to come back tomorrow I wonder if we could adjourn at this stage. It's a matter I need to address Your Honours on pretty urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I will have explained to you at the beginning of the day's session that one can't always predict the progress of these matters, and I know that you were all prepared to return home today, but as you would have gathered between what has passed between counsel and the Bench that your testimony still is not completed, and you would have to delay your return until tomorrow. And you would be required to attend the Tribunal again tomorrow. So you are now stood down as a witness but you're not excused, and I repeat the warnings that I would have given last week, that you cannot discuss your testimony with counsel from either side or with anyone outside of the chamber. So you are excused now to return tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
